overview: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Computer or Something Else? sits at the intersection of archaeology, astronomy, and the history of technology. Primary evidence comes from physical artifacts and peer-reviewed analyses rather than folklore.

timeline.event: Gear wheels noticed among recovered objects
Early reconstructions and CT-era studies begin
High-resolution imaging refines gear counts and inscriptions

key_discoveries: Complex bronze gear train inside a wooden case
Pointers consistent with calendrical and lunar predictions
competing_explanations: Hellenistic astronomical calculator for predicting eclipses and planetary positions
Earlier or parallel technological traditions not yet recovered
supporting_evidence: Inscribed text matching known Metonic and Saros cycles
Independent replications by researchers using CT data
contradictory_evidence: No other complete devices of this complexity from the same period have been found
Some gear counts remain debated due to corrosion
consensus: Scholarly consensus treats the Antikythera mechanism as a sophisticated Greek astronomical device of the Hellenistic period. Exact complete function and whether it is unique remain open.
unresolved_questions: Who built it and for whom?
Were similar devices common but lost to recycling of bronze?
How much of the original case and pointers are missing?

claims.text: The Antikythera mechanism was recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera around 1900–1901.
The device contains a complex system of bronze gears used for astronomical calculations.

sources.title: Nature research coverage of Antikythera studies
Scientific American reporting on CT analyses

claims.text: No other complete mechanism of equal complexity from the same era has been recovered.
claims.notes: Absence of evidence is not absolute proof of uniqueness.

claims.text: The mechanism could predict the positions of all known planets with modern accuracy.
claims.notes: Planetary modeling is supported for some cycles; full modern accuracy claims exceed consensus.
